comm.t: Medhas resumes for King Suratha and the merchant Samādhi. Niśumbha has fallen at the end of chapter 9; this chapter tells the last duel, between the Goddess and Śumbha, and closes the third story (Uttama Carita, chapters 5–13).

In the Gita Press pāṭha the chapter is preceded by its own dhyāna, which meditates on the Goddess as Kāmeśvarī, ‘the form of Śiva and Śakti’ (शिवशक्तिरूपां कामेश्वरीं). The dhyāna and the bīja ॐ that opens this mantra in recitation belong to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa.

samasa.sense: as dear to him as his own life

morph.note: Imperfect of √ब्रू, which inserts ī before consonantal endings in the strong forms: अ-ब्रव्-ई-त्. A favourite narrative past in the Purāṇas.
Present passive participle: passive stem हन्य- (√हन् + yak) + -मान. ‘Being killed’ — the slaughter is still going on.
Past participle of an intransitive root, active in sense: ‘having become angry’.

mantras.anvaya: भ्रातरं प्राणसम्मितं निशुम्भं निहतं, बलं च एव हन्यमानं दृष्ट्वा, क्रुद्धः शुम्भः वचः अब्रवीत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two objects with predicates (निशुम्भं निहतम्, बलं हन्यमानम्) depend on the absolutive दृष्ट्वा; the main clause is क्रुद्धः शुम्भः वचः अब्रवीत्.
mantras.lit: Śumbha, seeing his brother Niśumbha, dear as his own life, slain, and his army too being slaughtered, spoke words in anger.
mantras.tr: When Śumbha saw his brother Niśumbha, dear to him as life, lying slain, and his army being cut down, he spoke in fury.

comm.t: The link from chapter 9: Niśumbha is dead and the remaining army is being destroyed. Śumbha, now alone, addresses the Goddess directly.
A modern reading: the text gives the demon a human grief — the brother was ‘equal to his life’. The anger that follows grows out of loss as well as pride.

sandhi.note: Final t becomes d before the voiced d. The Gita Press writes the d with a virāma and a space.
Final m is not changed before a vowel; it simply joins the following ā. (Before a consonant it would be anusvāra, as in त्वं.)
ā + a → ā; the relative pronoun and its predicate fuse.

samasa.alt: Also बलेन अवलेपः, ‘conceit caused by strength’ (tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa); the sense is the same.

morph.note: मा with the imperative (मा … आवह) is the Epic and Purāṇic idiom for a prohibition; classical prose prefers मा with the unaugmented aorist.

√युध् is a divādi (4th class) ātmanepada root: stem युध्य-. The Gita Press spells it with a doubled dh (युद्ध्य-), an orthographic convention of doubling a consonant before y; the form is the ordinary युध्यसे.
Pronominal declension: अन्य takes -साम् in the feminine genitive plural, like सर्वासाम्, not the noun ending -आनाम्.

mantras.anvaya: दुष्टे दुर्गे, त्वं बलावलेपात् गर्वं मा आवह। या (त्वम्) अतिमानिनी (असि, सा त्वम्) अन्यासां बलम् आश्रित्य युद्ध्यसे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: a prohibition (मा … आवह) with a causal ablative, and an accusation whose subject is the relative या … अतिमानिनी (‘you, who are so proud’).
mantras.lit: O wicked Durgā, do not carry pride out of the arrogance of strength. You who are exceedingly proud fight relying on the strength of other (women).
mantras.tr: Wicked Durgā, do not swell with pride in your power! For all your arrogance, you fight leaning on the strength of others.
mantras.tr_note: या अतिमानिनी, literally ‘(you) who (are) exceedingly proud’, is rendered ‘for all your arrogance’.

comm.t: Śumbha’s taunt: the Goddess has not fought alone. The Mothers (Brahmāṇī and the others, 8.13 ff.) and Śivadūtī fought beside her in chapters 8–9, and Śumbha himself came to the field after they had fought (9.8). He calls this borrowed strength.
The charge prepares the answer of 10.5: what Śumbha sees as ‘others’ is the Goddess herself. The tradition reads the taunt as the demon’s error in its purest form — he sees many where there is one.
A modern reading: Śumbha’s accusation is the one we make of anyone whose strength we cannot explain — that it must come from somewhere else.

sandhi.note: ā + e → ai (एकैव); a + a → ā (एवाहम्). The final m becomes anusvāra before ज (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).

samasa.sense: the Mothers and Śivadūtī, who are the Goddess’s own powers; मद् is the compound stem of अस्मद् (मत्, voiced before v)

morph.note: Feminine nominative and accusative plural of एतद् have the same form. Here it must be nominative: it agrees with विशन्त्यः and मद्विभूतयः, which are nominative (the accusatives would be विशन्तीः, विभूतीः). After पश्य the clause is a direct exclamation: ‘Look — these … are entering me.’
Present participle of √विश् (stem विशत्), feminine विशन्ती, nominative plural; a participle used as the predicate: ‘are entering (as you watch)’.
Ordinal of द्वि. With का … अपरा the question means ‘what other, second (woman) is there besides me?’ — a rhetorical denial.

mantras.anvaya: अत्र जगति अहम् एका एव (अस्मि)। मम अपरा द्वितीया का (अस्ति)? दुष्ट, पश्य — एताः मद्विभूतयः मयि एव विशन्त्यः (सन्ति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A statement (एका एव अहम्), a rhetorical question (द्वितीया का मम अपरा), and an imperative introducing a nominal clause (पश्य — एताः … विशन्त्यः मद्विभूतयः).
mantras.lit: I am alone, one only, here in the world. What second, other than me, is there? O wicked one, look: these, my powers, are entering into me alone.
mantras.tr: I am alone in this world. Who else is there besides me? See, wicked one: these powers of mine are returning into me.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Entering’ is rendered ‘returning into’, since the powers came from her; the Sanskrit says only that they enter.

comm.t: The Goddess answers the charge of 10.3. The ‘others’ (अन्यासाम्) are not others: they are her own vibhūtis, and as she speaks they merge back into her (10.6). Śumbha has been fighting her all along.

In the Śākta tradition this verse is a central statement of the text’s non-dualism: the many goddesses are one Goddess, and the world holds no second power beside her. The same claim was made earlier in narrative form — the śaktis came out of the gods’ bodies in their forms (8.13) — and here the Goddess states it of herself.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has names that state the same idea: एकाकिनी (665, ‘the one who is alone’), निर्द्वैता (667) and द्वैतवर्जिता (668, ‘free of duality’). The hymns are separate works; the shared doctrine is common Śākta thought.

A modern reading: there is an echo of Śumbha’s own boast in 5.111, where he claimed that every jewel of the three worlds rests ‘in me alone’ (मय्येव). The Goddess uses the same words truthfully: what seemed to be many is gathered into one.
